finding.affected_callers: src/path_manager.cpp:1378,1734,1781,1934,1947,1953,1964,1979,1999,2013,2029,2413 (13 `visualization_->` uses); docs/design/planning_visualization_usage_ko.md:49 (`connection.tube(...)`); no tests, no examples, no other package (grep)

verdict.evidence:
The facts in the finding are correct. Each method is a `void ... const` whose only body is a publish call: ros_planning_visualization.cpp:23 `front_end_->publish(m)`, :24-31 `tube` routes to opt_/global_/front_tube_, :32-38 the rest, and :33 `pipeline` publishes only when `pipeline_` is non-null. Publishers are transient_local/reliable depth 1 (cpp:6). The sibling layer does use publish verbs: path_manager.h:722 `publishEffectiveRiskField`, :723 `publishRiskHeatmap`, :729 `publishTrajRisk`, :738 `publishTubeMarker`, :758 `publishRiskProfile`.

Several things lessen the problem. (a) The class comment at h:7-8 ("Concrete ROS connection only. Publishers keep their original topic/QoS; messages are prepared separately") and the class name together say that the class only publishes. (b) Every method returns `void` and takes a prepared ROS message, so reading `riskHeatmap(msg)` as a getter or `tube(...)` as a builder does not survive a look at the signature. The builders sit in a separate namespace and all use the `make*` prefix (e.g. path_manager.cpp:1945 `visualization::makeTube`), which keeps the two roles apart. (c) Every production call sits inside a `PathManager::publishX` wrapper, so the case cited at path_manager.cpp:1947 is inside `publishTubeMarker` (cpp:1939), and the others are inside `publishPipelineDebug` (:1927), `publishTrajTube` (:1956) and `publishRiskHeatmap` (:2008). A reviewer reading those lines already sees "publish". (d) Two other audit notes already rated this optional or low: docs/design/api_naming_audit_2026_10_12/orchestration_review.md:39 and public_api_review.md:125.

One point adds to the cost. The header is installed (CMakeLists.txt:782 `install(DIRECTORY include/`), it is part of exported `path_manager_lib` (CMakeLists.txt:697), and it is pulled in by path_manager.h:21. A rename is therefore technically a break of the installed API, even though no consumer is known. The usage doc docs/design/planning_visualization_usage_ko.md:49 shows `connection.tube(TubeChannel::Optimized, *tube)` under the heading "발행하기" ("Publishing"), which spells out the publish meaning there.

The `const` qualifier is a fair minor point: publishing has an external effect, yet the methods are const. This follows the usual rclcpp pattern of a const method calling through a shared_ptr publisher, so it is not a contract violation.
verdict.note:
Weakened, not refuted. The ambiguity is real but small, and the void signatures, the class comment, the make* split and the publishX wrappers around every call already resolve it in practice.

Call counts (src/, excluding reports/, experiments/ and the archived docs/validation snapshots):
- 11 production calls to the noun methods, all in path_manager.cpp: 1378, 1734, 1781, 1934, 1947, 1964, 1979, 1999, 2013, 2029, 2413. The finding's 12 also counts clearTrajectory at 1953. pipelineEnabled (1931) and the constructor (369) are not counted.
- 0 tests. test/planning_visualization_test.cpp and examples/planning_visualization_example.cpp exercise only the make* builders and never this class.
- No other package refers to it.

The docs/validation/planning_visualization_2026_10_10 overlay.patch and source/current snapshot also contain these names, but they are frozen evidence. Leave them unchanged under either option.

Cheapest fix: add one header comment, e.g. "Each method publishes the given prepared message on its fixed latched topic (transient_local, depth 1); no state is read or retained". This avoids churn in an installed header.

If the team renames anyway, do it as one batch: publishFrontEndPath, publishTube, publishChain, publishPipeline, publishTrajectoryRisk, publishRiskProfile, publishRiskHeatmap, publishRiskField, publishDynamicObstacles. It touches 11 call lines plus planning_visualization_usage_ko.md:49, and it is better done before anyone outside the package depends on the installed header. Low priority either way.

There is no bug suspicion. clearTrajectory (cpp:39-44) matches the scope its comment documents at h:23 and in usage doc line 51.

verdict.symbol: using namespace ego_planner; (file-scope using-directive in installed header)
verdict.evidence:
The facts check out. path_manager.h:46 `using namespace ego_planner;` sits at global scope, before `namespace path_manager` at :48, and has no comment. It is the only using-directive in any .h/.hpp under src outside docs/validation copies (grep "using namespace"). The header is installed by path_manager/CMakeLists.txt:782 `install(DIRECTORY include/ DESTINATION include)` and exported with :806 `ament_export_targets(export_${PROJECT_NAME} ...)`, and its INSTALL_INTERFACE include is at :151-153.

The header itself depends on the directive. Unqualified ego_planner names appear at path_manager.h:148 `const LocalTrajData &executionTrajectory()`, :149 `const GlobalTrajData &referenceTrajectory()`, :353 and :357 `SwarmTrajData`, and :785 `SwarmTrajData swarm_trajectories_;`. These types come from plan_container.hpp:11-45 (namespace ego_planner). replan_fsm.cpp:616 `const LocalTrajData *info` also relies on it. Every other use is already qualified (`ego_planner::TailBoundary` at :120/:132/:154, `ego_planner::PolyTrajOptimizer` at :184/:209/:887). So the fix is about 6 qualifications, not 3 sources.

The finding is incomplete in two ways. First, the same installed include chain has worse global leaks. path_optimizer/include/path_optimizer/poly_traj_optimizer.h:14 has a global `using LogManager = swarm_formation::LogManager;`, and :24-47 define global, unprefixed `LOG_INFO`/`LOG_WARN`/`LOG_ERROR` macros with no #undef anywhere. plan_container.hpp:9 has a global `using std::vector;`. path_manager.h:7-8 includes both files. Second, no example or out-of-package consumer includes path_manager.h. examples/mission_planner_example.cpp:3-4 includes only mission_planner.h and ros_planning_backend.h. ros_planning_backend.h:11 forward-declares `class PathManager;`, and mission_planner.h:3-4 does not include it. The "66 explicit uses" count is also off: grep -c gives 53 in path_manager.cpp, replan_fsm.cpp and segment_chain_planner.cpp, and 35 in the three headers.
verdict.note:
This is a real installed-header hygiene problem, not a rename. I downgraded it because no example or external consumer includes path_manager.h today. Its 7 production translation units are all in-package: 4 include it directly (path_manager.cpp, ros_planning_backend.cpp, replan_fsm.h, segment_chain_planner.h) and 3 get it transitively (replan_fsm.cpp, segment_chain_planner.cpp, node.cpp). The 19 test files are also in-package: 14 include it directly and 5 through replan_fsm.h or segment_chain_planner.h. The documented public consumer path (mission_planner.h + ros_planning_backend.h) forward-declares PathManager and avoids the leak.

The example in the finding (an ambiguous TailBoundary/PolyTrajOptimizer name) is possible but hypothetical. A narrow fix is cheap: qualify path_manager.h:148,149,353,357,785 and replan_fsm.cpp:616 with ego_planner::, then delete :46. It still needs a compile check, because test files may also use unqualified ego_planner names, which I did not grep exhaustively.

If header hygiene is taken up, it should be one item covering the larger leaks in the same chain. The global unprefixed LOG_INFO/LOG_WARN/LOG_ERROR macros (poly_traj_optimizer.h:24-47) are more likely to collide with a consumer's own logging macros than the using-directive is. Also in scope: the global LogManager alias (poly_traj_optimizer.h:14) and `using std::vector;` (plan_container.hpp:9). That combined item would deserve medium priority. On its own, this directive is low.

finding.issue: Overlaps another reviewer's area but the example exposes it. `clean{true}` defaults to true while `evaluated{false}`; unflyable() returns false when !evaluated (evaluated && ...). So an unevaluated report reads 'clean and not unflyable'. The example prints clean before checking evaluated (flight_evaluator_example.cpp:29-30) and only the final return guards it (:36); README.md:51-53 has to warn users explicitly.
finding.misreading_example: A caller who only tests `!report.verdict.unflyable()` or `report.verdict.clean` accepts a malformed or degenerate trajectory (evaluated=false, issue=DEGENERATE_INPUT) as flyable.
finding.reason: The names are right for the evaluated case; the hazard is the unevaluated default and the missing tri-state. Options that are not renames: add `bool flyable() const { return evaluated && !unflyable(); }`/`isClean()` helpers, or document the default prominently in the header. Existing semantics must stay for the 24 callers (.unflyable() in flight_evaluator_test 7, segment_chain_planner 5, chain_experiment_test 4, example 1; `.clean` 11 refs).
finding.affected_callers: 24 `.unflyable()` refs and 11 `.clean` refs (flight_evaluator_test.cpp, segment_chain_planner.cpp, chain_experiment_test.cpp, route_search_backend_test.cpp, flight_evaluator.cpp, example)

verdict.evidence: Defaults: flight_evaluation.h:29 `bool evaluated{false};  // false: degenerate input, nothing was judged`, :30 `bool clean{true};` (no comment on the default). :73-76 `bool unflyable() const { return evaluated && (...); }`. The doc comment above it (:66-72) ends "the flight was not checked, so it is not cleared". That describes !policy_measurable, but a reader can take it as the rule for unevaluated input too, and the `evaluated &&` guard does the opposite. unflyableMeasured() (:85-88) has the same guard. In the implementation, `clean` is assigned only together with `evaluated = true` (flight_evaluator.cpp:469-473). On DEGENERATE_INPUT/INVALID_TRAJECTORY (flight_evaluator.cpp:16,22,26) the verdict keeps clean=true and unflyable()=false. The codebase has already been caught by this twice: segment_chain_planner.cpp:566-569 ("!evaluated must fail too. unflyable() is false when nothing was judged ... the exact fail-open this gate exists to remove") and :3141-3145 ("review find: unflyable() is false when evaluated is false, so a malformed span set slid a stitched product through as SUCCESS"). The warning appears only outside the header: examples/library_consumer/README.md:52 and docs/design/planning_computation_usage_ko.md:178. The example prints `clean` before any evaluated check (flight_evaluator_example.cpp:29-30) and guards only in its return (:36). The disambiguating field `FlightEvaluationReport::issue` exists (flight_evaluator.h:162-163), but FlightVerdict is also passed around on its own (evaluateFlightInContext returns a bare verdict, segment_chain_planner.cpp:562), and then `issue` is not available.
verdict.note: The finding holds as a contract problem, not a naming problem. Both names are accurate when the verdict has been evaluated, so no rename is needed. The hazard is factually real, and the planner's own code hit it twice; the fail-open comments at segment_chain_planner.cpp:566 and :3141 show this. The misreading is plausible: someone reading only the header sees `clean{true}` and a `unflyable()` whose doc comment promises "not checked => not cleared". Correction to the claimed counts: the 24 `unflyable()` refs include comment lines and the definition. Real code call sites are 17. Production has 5, all in segment_chain_planner.cpp (569, 682, 2103, 3083, 3166). The example has 1 (:36). Tests have 11: flight_evaluator_test.cpp has 7 (132, 266, 282, 303, 308, 318, 350) and chain_experiment_test.cpp has 4 (1837, 2671, 4142, 4203). `.clean` code refs are 11 lines. Production has 3: flight_evaluator.cpp:473 (write) and :607, plus segment_chain_planner.cpp:2103. The example has 1 (:30). Tests have 7 refs: flight_evaluator_test.cpp has 6 (111, 272, 275, 290, 308, 314) and route_search_backend_test.cpp:415 has 1 line with 2 refs. caller_count=10 counts production plus example call sites (5+3+1+1), and test_references=20 counts lines (11 unflyable + 9 clean, where chain_experiment test lines are counted once). Further copies sit in docs/validation/*/main.cpp, which are frozen consumer snapshots and not counted. Ways to fix it without renaming, cheapest first: (1) Document the header. Add a comment on `clean{true}` saying it is meaningful only when evaluated. Add a note on unflyable()/unflyableMeasured() that they return false for unevaluated input and that callers must check `evaluated` first. Copy the README.md:52 warning into the header. (2) Add a non-breaking helper, e.g. `bool cleared() const { return evaluated && clean && !unflyable(); }` or `flyable()`, and switch the example to it. (3) Changing the default to `clean{false}` would also fail closed, but it changes the observable default on unevaluated reports. That needs runtime re-verification against flight_evaluator_test and the docs/validation consumer JSON baselines before it is considered. Keep the existing `unflyable()` semantics: segment_chain_planner.cpp:2101-2103 and the unflyableMeasured() split depend on the current graded meaning.

verdict.evidence: The claim checks out. trajectory_simulation.hpp:164 declares `SimulationControl controller(double time_s, const SimulationState &state) const;`. The only nearby comment is hpp:161, "Playback uses the same controller/model arithmetic as integration." It is a group comment and does not say what this method returns, so it does not clear up the confusion. The class's other noun-named methods are plain getters: `reference()` returns `input_.reference` (hpp:160), and `states()`, `metrics()` and `status()` are also getters (hpp:156-158). `SimulationInput::controller` (hpp:125, `TrackingController::Ptr`) is an input field with the same name. So by the pattern of its own class, `controller()` reads like a getter for that field. In fact it is a computation (cpp:269-275): sampleReference(time_s), then stateVelocity, then `input_.controller->commandedAcceleration(ref, state, velocity)`, then `input_.model->realize(state, command)`. It returns the control after the model has realized it (thrust_n/lift_n/bank_rad/drag_n/acceleration_mps2, `state_representable`; hpp:45-49), not the raw commanded acceleration. The finding's claim of a silent bug through `auto` is overstated. SimulationControl has no `commandedAcceleration`, so any attempt to use it as a controller fails to compile. There is no silent runtime misuse.
caller_examples: doc mention: mmp_path_planning/docs/transition_phase_contract.md:277 (`derivative()` -> `controller()`, describes the older node structure)
verdict.note: I confirm the naming problem. I lowered priority from medium to low because misuse fails at compile time and no code outside the class calls the method. Reference counts (rg `\bcontroller\s*\(` over src, reports/experiments excluded): 1 declaration, 1 definition, 2 internal calls inside SimulationSession's own methods, 1 test call, and 0 calls from other production code or examples. dynamics_sim_node playback never calls it directly.
